title: Joan of Arc (1412–1431)
hook: a farm girl who led armies, was burned at nineteen, and was declared innocent 25 years later

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, who called the pope sweet daddy and told him, lovingly, to come home. Your line was be who god meant.

France, 1429, deep in a war with England that has dragged on for generations. A peasant girl of about seventeen, from a village in the east, who can't read or write, walks into the court of the uncrowned king. God has sent her, she tells him, to lift the siege of Orléans and see him crowned. Nobody expects her, and plenty doubt her. She has no title and no training. Within a few months, the siege is lifted and the king is crowned.
screen: `FRANCE, AT WAR.` → `A FARM GIRL AT COURT.` → `ORLÉANS, 1429.`

segments.voice: Joan said that from about the age of thirteen she heard voices, which she identified as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to go and help the king. She cut her hair, put on armor, and rode at the front of the army carrying a banner. At her trial she said she loved her banner far more than her sword, and carried it so she wouldn't have to kill anyone. The siege of Orléans broke. That summer the king was crowned at Reims, with Joan beside him. Then it fell apart. A year later she was captured and sold to the English, who tried her before a church court run by a bishop on their side. She had no lawyer. For months, learned men tried to trap her. One trap became famous: are you in God's grace? Say yes, and she's proud. Say no, and she's condemned herself. A nineteen-year-old with no schooling answered, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there, and if I am, may God keep me there. By later accounts, her questioners were stunned. They burned her anyway, in Rouen, in 1431. She asked for a cross to be held up where she could see it. Twenty-five years later, with the pope's approval, a new church trial declared the first one unjust and cleared her name. In 1920 she was declared a saint. So the same Church that condemned her, through a bishop, later admitted it was wrong and honored her. Today's line, I am not afraid, is a saying people hang on her; that exact sentence isn't in the trial records. What the records do hold is a teenager answering learned men for months without backing down.
screen: `VOICES, AND A BANNER.` · `ORLÉANS FREED, A KING CROWNED.` · `ARE YOU IN GOD'S GRACE?` · `CONDEMNED, THEN CLEARED.` · then, large: `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you know what's right but have stayed quiet, at work, in your family, among friends, and notice whether fear sits somewhere in your body. Don't push it away; Joan wept at her trial, and kept answering. Picture one small step you could take, and if you pray, ask for her courage.
Orléans. The besieged city Joan of Arc helped free, months before the king's crowning and her own capture.
Your line: I am not afraid. Whoever first said it, Joan lived it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Joan of Arc on 30 May; she is one of the patron saints of France, and many ask her prayers for courage.

notes: All Joan material paraphrased from the trial records; the grace answer is given 'in effect' without quotation marks, since no approved public-domain translation was used.

The index carry 'I am not afraid' comes from a popular attribution ('I am not afraid... I was born to do this') not found in the trial records; the script says so. Keeper may want the index carry reconsidered.
Banner vs sword: trial session of 27 February 1431 ('forty times' more than her sword). Confirm.
Orléans siege lifted 8 May 1429 (Joan arrived 29 April); coronation at Reims 17 July 1429; captured at Compiègne May 1430; burned 30 May 1431 in Rouen. Confirm.
The tribunal was presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon, aligned with the English; the 1456 nullification was authorized by Pope Callixtus III. Confirm.
Canonized 16 May 1920 by Benedict XV. Confirm.
Final condemnation was for relapsed heresy (resuming male clothing), not witchcraft. Confirm.
The court's reaction to the grace answer ('the room went quiet') was softened to 'by later accounts, her questioners were stunned', from nullification-trial testimony. Confirm.
Her birth year (c. 1412) is traditional, so 'seventeen' in 1429 and 'nineteen' at her death are approximate.
She was captured by Burgundian forces and handed to the English for payment; 'sold to the English' compresses that. Confirm.
'She cried at her trial' — accounts mention her weeping (e.g. at the threat of burning, and at Saint-Ouen). Confirm.
